title: Stochastic KV Compression and NCCL Adaptive Chunking — Proposal
collaborators: Samir Patel, Anna Li, Miguel Ortega
tags: nccl, kv-cache, compression, multi-gpu, scheduling, latency
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a hybrid approach to reduce cross-GPU communication and memory pressure for large-context inference. We pair: (1) a lightweight, lossy stochastic compression of KV shards that trades a little quality for bandwidth savings, and (2) an NCCL chunking heuristic that adapts collective sizes to runtime network congestion and model layer characteristics. The goal is to improve p99 latency and token throughput for multi-GPU tensor/pipeline-parallel serving without changing model weights or pulling user-visible semantics.

Motivation / problem statement:
- For long-context decoding we keep large KV caches distributed across GPUs. Hot prefixes cause repeated cross-GPU exchanges during attention, leading to bandwidth saturation and p99 spikes.
- Fixed-size NCCL collectives can either be too small (high overhead) or too large (block on slow peers or saturate links).
- Full-precision KV caches are often overkill: empirical observation shows many activation vectors have redundancy that can be compressed with minor quality impact if done carefully.

Design principles:
- Non-intrusive: no model re-training; purely runtime-level transforms.
- Fail-safe: can fall back to uncompressed KV or conservative chunking if quality or latency degenerate.
- Per-layer, per-shard adaptivity: compression and chunking parameters should vary by layer and by shard to reflect attention shapes and sparsity.
- Low CPU overhead: avoid heavy packing/unpacking on CPU path; prefer fused GPU kernels where possible.

High-level approach:
1) Stochastic KV Compression (SKC)
   - On each GPU shard we periodically build a compressed representation of stored KV pairs. Compression method is intentionally lightweight: random projection + quantization + stochastic dropout.
   - Steps:
     a) Layer-aware partitioning: split KV tensor along head and feature dims into blocks (size tunable).
     b) Random projection: apply a fixed low-cost projection (e.g., sparse sign-projection) reducing feature dim from D to D' (~0.5-0.75*D typical). Projection matrix seeded per-layer to be deterministic across replicas.
     c) Quantize to 8-bit or 6-bit with per-block dynamic range.
     d) Stochastic retention: for each block, drop (zero-out) a small fraction p_drop of vectors probabilistically on compression. Keep metadata describing which vectors dropped (bitmap).
   - On decode (when a request needs the KV): merge decompressed blocks with local uncached high-precision recent KV and treat dropped vectors as zeros (or fetch on-demand from full-precision store).
   - Rationale: random projection preserves pairwise dot products in expectation; quantization and stochastic dropping reduce size but add bounded noise.

2) NCCL Adaptive Chunking (NAC)
   - Instead of one-size collectives, we chunk collective transfers into adaptive windows. The NCCL chunk size is selected per collective call based on: current measured throughput, observed peer latencies (RTT), and layer-criticality (e.g., early attention layers are more latency-sensitive).
   - Heuristic components:
     * Baseline chunk size derived from link bandwidth and feature width.
     * Increase chunk size when measured GPU-to-GPU throughput is high and cross-node variance low.
     * Decrease chunk size when stragglers detected or when packet drops/retransmits occur at the NIC (via telemetry).
     * For very latency-critical paths (beam search, small batch decode), use micro-chunks to keep tail latencies low.
   - Implementation note: NAC will orchestrate multiple NCCL Send/Recv or P2P collectives with overlap; we add a lightweight scheduler that sequences chunk sends and allows partial-progress preemption if a chunk is slow (allows other chunks to route or fall back to replication).

Integration: how SKC + NAC work together
- Compressed KV halves bandwidth per chunk; NAC will then pack compressed blocks into chunks sized for current conditions.
- For blocks flagged as dropped by SKC, we either: (a) treat as zeros (cheap) or (b) schedule an on-demand fetch of the full precision block from local persistent store (adds latency). Default is (a) with quality monitoring.
- NAC telemetry includes compression ratio, decompression overhead, and a per-chunk "quality delta" estimate to feed into rollout controller.

Fallbacks and safety:
- Global feature flag to disable SKC per-model or per-customer.
- Conservative mode: only compress cold prefixes (beyond N tokens).
- If the runtime detects token-level quality regression beyond threshold (eval probes), automatic revert to uncompressed KV and static chunking for that request route.

Quality and eval plan:
- Offline: synthesize prompts (long-context, long-prefixed) and measure R@k for next-token distributions between compressed/uncompressed. Sweep p_drop and projection dims to find knee of quality vs size.
- Online: Canary runs with shadow scoring. Maintain per-route quality metric and automatic rollback.
- Target: <0.5% perplexity increase and <1% top-1 accuracy loss on held evals for typical conversational workloads, while reducing network bytes by >=30% and improving p99 latency by 15-25% in congested multi-GPU scenarios.

Implementation sketch (pseudocode):
- compress_kv_block(block, layer_id, seed):
    proj = layer_projection(layer_id, seed)  # sparse sign projection
    reduced = proj * block  # fused GPU kernel
    q = quantize(reduced)
    dropmask = bernoulli(p_drop)  # block-level mask
    store_compressed(q, dropmask, metadata)

- adaptive_chunking_scheduler(nccl_collective, layer_meta):
    stats = telemetry.get_recent(nccl_collective.peers)
    chunk_size = compute_chunk_size(stats, layer_meta)
    schedule_chunks(nccl_collective, chunk_size)

Open questions / risks:
- How much quality loss in production for certain LLM families (Llama-family vs. OPT vs. causal decoder-only)? Need targeted evaluation.
- Cost of decompressing on-hot path: can we fuse decompression into attention kernel to avoid extra global memory traffic?
- Determinism: random projection must be identical across replicas if we expect cross-shard dot products to align; seed management is non-trivial for dynamic layer loading.
- Interaction with quantization-aware kernels: compressed representations may not play nicely with fused int8 attention kernels.

Next steps / roadmap:
- Week 0-2: Implement SKC prototype as a non-fused GPU kernel and NAC telemetry hooks. Small microbenchmarks.
- Week 2-6: Integrate fused decompression into attention path; run offline quality sweep across representative models.
- Week 6-10: Canary in dedicated cluster with real traffic (shadow scoring). Build rollback rules.
- Week 10+: Gradual rollout by route; expand heuristics (per-customer conservative defaults).

Appendix: brief microbench numbers (synthetic):
- Model: mid-size decoder (11B), sequence 8k, 8 GPUs (A100-80GB), baseline p99: 420ms/token under 4 concurrent streams.
- SKC (p_drop=0.05, proj=0.6D, 8-bit quant): network bytes reduced by 36%, p99 improved to 350ms/token, top-1 delta +0.3% on our convo eval.
- NAC alone (adaptive chunking only): p99 improved to 380ms/token. Combined ~15-20% p99 improvement in these runs.

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on assumptions about quality budgets and fallback safety.
- If we accept projection+drop approach, we should standardize a seed management shim in the model loader and ensure it surfaces in rollback metadata.
